title: Minister for Social Care writes to Councils to accelerate Motor Neurone Disease (MND) Care Access
authors: Iain MacBeath, Adult Social Care Delivery Senior Advisor, the Department of Health and Social Care

content.text: Following Baroness Casey’s recommendation in her Nuffield Trust speech in March this year, the Minister for Social Care has written to local authorities to encourage the fast-tracking of access to care for people with motor neurone disease (MND), ahead of wider reform.

"As you will know, Baroness Casey is chairing an independent commission into adult social care, reporting into the Prime Minister. Baroness Casey made a number of immediate recommendations in March this year, including a recommendation to fast track access to care and support for people with Motor Neurone Disease.

The Minister set out the immediate initial steps we are inviting local authorities to take to streamline and accelerate access to care and support for people with Motor Neurone Disease within existing frameworks, ahead of fuller collaborative reform.

Motor Neurone Disease is a severe, progressive and terminal condition that requires rapid, responsive care as needs quickly evolve. As part of her review, Baroness Casey heard directly from people with personal experience of Motor Neurone Disease about delays in accessing the right care and support, and the profound impact this can have on individuals and their families, including avoidable crises, hospital admissions, and a loss of independence and dignity…

… It is essential that services respond with pace, coordination and foresight to keep up with escalating and complex needs. The Department of Health and Social Care is already taking forward Baroness Casey’s recommendation at pace, working in partnership with the Motor Neurone Disease Association, as well as extensively across local government representatives, the NHS, wider sector partners, and drawing on the experiences of people with Motor Neurone Disease, to develop ways of driving both immediate improvements and more substantial reform.

In the meantime, there is immediate scope for many areas to better meet the needs of people with Motor Neurone Disease within existing frameworks and partnerships, including through prioritising timely, straightforward assessment processes and delivering coordinated, responsive care and support…

… Finally, while the letter focuses on Motor Neurone Disease as one of the most acute and time critical conditions, I would encourage you to consider how these approaches might also apply to people with similarly rapidly progressing needs."
